sourceNote: Topic and subtopic headings, their numbering and the Core/Supplement split of every learning statement are transcribed from the official syllabus document. Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase; each objective code is the subtopic code plus the board's own statement number (Core statements first, then Supplement). 'Supplement:' marks statements examined only on the Extended papers (2 and 4).
notes: Checked on 2026-10-07 against the official PDF (version 2, published August 2026; 'Content overview', 'Assessment overview', 'Subject content', 'Details of the assessment' and 'Changes to this syllabus'): all 12 topics and 49 subtopic headings, their numbering, the Core/Supplement split of every statement and the paper facts match.

Supplement-only subtopic: 2.7 Metallic bonding (the Core column is empty), linked to Papers 2 and 4. These subtopics have Core statements only: 2.1, 2.2, 3.2, 6.1, 8.2, 8.3, 8.5, 9.1, 9.2, 10.1, 10.2, 11.3, 12.1, 12.2, 12.4 and 12.5. In 3.3 only statement 1 (units of concentration) is Core; all the mole calculations are Supplement.

A node cannot restrict a concept by tier, so Supplement depth is recorded in the objectives ('Supplement:') and in the concept descriptions of content/concepts/chemistry-o.json; content written for Supplement statements must say so.

Practical skills (Papers 5 and 6, 20%) are not a numbered subject-content subtopic: section 4 'Practical assessment' lists the experimental contexts (simple quantitative measurements, rates, salt preparation, filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation, chromatography, electrolysis, identification of ions and gases, tests for water, test-tube reactions of dilute acids including ethanoic acid, tests for oxidising and reducing agents, heating and cooling curves, titrations, solubility, melting and boiling points, displacement reactions of metals and halogens, temperature changes, conditions for rusting) and the skills (planning, measuring, recording, interpreting, evaluating). These skills are covered by the concepts on 12.1 (apparatus and measurement; planning investigations; recording, presenting and evaluating data).

The 'Notes for use in qualitative analysis' (tests and results for anions, aqueous cations with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia, gases and flame colours) are provided in Papers 5 and 6; content for 12.5 must give exactly those results. Mathematical requirements: calculators may be used in all parts of the examination; gradients from a tangent to a curve are for Extended candidates only.

Paper facts are from 'Assessment overview' and 'Details of the assessment'. Version 2 (August 2026) changed only the Assessment overview on page 9 and states that there are no substantial changes affecting teaching; textbooks endorsed for examination from 2023 remain suitable.
The development database has an older demo IGCSE Chemistry syllabus (versionLabel demo-development, isDemo, effective 2000-01-01); publishing this version as CURRENT supersedes it, which is intended.

ZIMSEC-only concepts of the family registry (simple cells and the lead-acid battery, measuring enthalpy changes, the Ostwald process, Group II, lime, mineral ores and processing, coal and diamond processing, separation of air, types of fuels, fuel efficiency, fuels from coal, wood and biomass, soaps, the ozone layer, hard water, waste, herbs) are deliberately not covered by this syllabus.
overview: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry builds knowledge and understanding of chemical facts, theories and practice: states of matter, atomic structure and bonding, stoichiometry, electrochemistry, energetics, rates, equilibrium and redox, acids, bases and salts, the Periodic Table, metals, the chemistry of the environment, organic chemistry and chemical analysis. It also develops experimental skills, data handling and problem solving in familiar and unfamiliar contexts. All candidates study the Core content; Extended candidates also study the Supplement. The course is designed for about 130 guided learning hours.
assessmentOverview: All candidates take three papers. Core candidates (grades C to G) take Paper 1 (multiple choice, 45 minutes, 40 marks, 30%) and Paper 3 (theory, 1 hour 15 minutes, 80 marks, 50%). Extended candidates (grades A* to G) take Paper 2 (multiple choice, 45 minutes, 40 marks, 30%) and Paper 4 (theory, 1 hour 15 minutes, 80 marks, 50%). Every candidate also takes one practical paper worth 20%: Paper 5 (Practical Test, 1 hour 15 minutes, 40 marks) or Paper 6 (Alternative to Practical, 1 hour, 40 marks). Papers 1 to 4 assess knowledge with understanding (AO1) and handling information and problem solving (AO2); Papers 5 and 6 assess experimental skills and investigations (AO3). Calculators may be used in all papers.

components.name: Paper 1: Multiple Choice (Core)
components.description: 40 compulsory four-option multiple-choice items on the Core content (AO1 and AO2).

components.name: Paper 2: Multiple Choice (Extended)
components.description: 40 compulsory four-option multiple-choice items on the Core and Supplement content (AO1 and AO2).

components.name: Paper 3: Theory (Core)
components.description: Compulsory short-answer and structured questions on the Core content (AO1 and AO2).

components.name: Paper 4: Theory (Extended)
components.description: Compulsory short-answer and structured questions on the Core and Supplement content (AO1 and AO2).

components.name: Paper 5: Practical Test
components.description: Compulsory practical tasks carried out in a laboratory, assessing experimental skills (AO3). An alternative to Paper 6 for Core and Extended candidates.

components.name: Paper 6: Alternative to Practical
components.description: Written questions on experimental skills (AO3) with no experiments to carry out. An alternative to Paper 5 for Core and Extended candidates.

routes.name: Core
routes.description: Papers 1 and 3 and one practical paper (5 or 6). Grades C to G are available.

routes.name: Extended
routes.description: Papers 2 and 4 and one practical paper (5 or 6). Grades A* to G are available.

objectives.text: State how solids, liquids and gases differ in their properties.
Describe the arrangement, separation and movement of the particles in solids, liquids and gases.
Describe melting, boiling, evaporating, freezing and condensing as changes of state.
Describe how the volume of a gas changes when its temperature or pressure changes.
Supplement: explain changes of state using the kinetic particle theory, including what heating and cooling curves show.
Supplement: use the kinetic particle theory to explain how temperature and pressure affect the volume of a gas.
Describe diffusion and explain it using the kinetic particle theory.
Supplement: describe and explain how the relative molecular mass of a gas affects how fast it diffuses.
Describe how elements, compounds and mixtures differ.

children.name: Atomic structure and the Periodic Table

objectives.text: Describe an atom as a central nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons arranged in shells around it.
State the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
Define proton (atomic) number as the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Define mass (nucleon) number as the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Work out the electronic configuration of atoms and ions of the elements with proton numbers 1 to 20 (for example 2,8,3).

State that the Group VIII noble gases have full outer shells, that the number of outer-shell electrons equals the group number for Groups I to VII, and that the number of occupied shells equals the period number.
Define isotopes as atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Interpret and write nuclide symbols, showing mass number and proton number, for atoms and ions.
Supplement: state that isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons and so the same electronic configuration.
Supplement: calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from the relative masses and abundances of its isotopes.
Describe how positive ions (cations) and negative ions (anions) are formed.
State that an ionic bond is a strong electrostatic attraction between ions of opposite charge.
Describe, using dot-and-cross diagrams, how ionic bonds form between elements of Group I and Group VII.
Describe the properties of ionic compounds: high melting and boiling points, and good electrical conductivity when molten or in aqueous solution but poor conductivity when solid.
Supplement: describe the giant lattice of an ionic compound as a regular arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions.
Supplement: describe, using dot-and-cross diagrams, the formation of ionic bonds between ions of metallic and non-metallic elements.
Supplement: explain the melting points, boiling points and electrical conductivity of ionic compounds in terms of their structure and bonding.
State that a covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons, giving the atoms noble-gas electronic configurations.
Describe covalent bonding in simple molecules including H₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CH₄, NH₃ and HCl, and draw dot-and-cross diagrams for these and similar molecules.
Describe, in terms of structure and bonding, why simple molecular compounds have low melting and boiling points and poor electrical conductivity.
Supplement: describe covalent bonding in molecules including CH₃OH, C₂H₄, O₂, CO₂ and N₂, and draw dot-and-cross diagrams for these and similar molecules.

Supplement: explain the low melting and boiling points of simple molecular compounds in terms of weak intermolecular forces (the types of force are not required), and explain their poor electrical conductivity.
Describe the giant covalent structures of graphite and diamond.
Relate the structure and bonding of graphite and diamond to their uses: graphite as a lubricant and as an electrode, and diamond in cutting tools.
Supplement: describe the giant covalent structure of silicon(IV) oxide, SiO₂.
Supplement: describe how the properties of silicon(IV) oxide resemble those of diamond and relate this to their structures.

children.name: Metallic bonding
children.description: Supplement content only: examined on the Extended papers.

objectives.text: Supplement: describe metallic bonding as the electrostatic attraction between the positive ions in a giant metallic lattice and a 'sea' of delocalised electrons.
Supplement: explain the good electrical conductivity, malleability and ductility of metals in terms of their structure and bonding.
State the formulae of the elements and compounds named in the syllabus.
Define the molecular formula of a compound as the number and type of each atom in one molecule.
Deduce the formula of a simple compound from the numbers of each type of atom shown in a model or diagram.
Write word equations and symbol equations, including state symbols, to show how reactants form products.
Supplement: define the empirical formula of a compound as the simplest whole-number ratio of the different atoms or ions in it.
Supplement: deduce the formula of an ionic compound from a model or diagram of its ions, or from the charges on the ions.
Supplement: write symbol equations with state symbols, including ionic equations.
Supplement: deduce the symbol equation, with state symbols, for a reaction from information given.

children.name: Relative masses of atoms and molecules

objectives.text: Describe relative atomic mass, Ar, as the average mass of the isotopes of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
Define relative molecular mass, Mr, as the sum of the relative atomic masses (relative formula mass for ionic compounds), and calculate it from a formula.
Calculate reacting masses in simple proportion, without using the mole.

children.name: The mole and the Avogadro constant
children.description: Statement 1 is Core; all mole calculations (statements 2 to 8) are Supplement.

objectives.text: State that concentration can be measured in g/dm³ or mol/dm³.
Supplement: state that the mole (mol) is the unit of amount of substance and that one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (atoms, ions or molecules), the Avogadro constant.

Supplement: use amount of substance (mol) = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol) to calculate an amount, a mass, a molar mass, a relative atomic or molecular/formula mass, or (with the Avogadro constant) a number of particles.
Supplement: use the molar gas volume, 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.), in calculations on gases.
Supplement: calculate reacting masses, limiting reactants, volumes of gases at r.t.p., volumes of solutions and concentrations in g/dm³ and mol/dm³, converting between cm³ and dm³.
Supplement: use titration results to calculate the amount of solute, or the concentration or volume of a solution.
Supplement: calculate empirical and molecular formulae from suitable data.
Supplement: calculate percentage yield, percentage composition by mass and percentage purity from suitable data.
Define electrolysis as the breaking down of an ionic compound, molten or in aqueous solution, by passing an electric current through it.
Identify the anode (positive electrode), the cathode (negative electrode) and the electrolyte (the molten or aqueous substance being electrolysed) in a simple electrolytic cell.

Identify the products at each electrode, and describe what is observed, when molten lead(II) bromide, concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and dilute sulfuric acid are electrolysed with inert platinum or carbon (graphite) electrodes.
State that metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and that non-metals other than hydrogen form at the anode.
Predict the products at each electrode when a molten binary compound is electrolysed.
State that metal objects are electroplated to improve their appearance and their resistance to corrosion.
Describe how a metal object is electroplated.
Supplement: describe how charge is transferred during electrolysis: electrons moving in the external circuit, electrons lost or gained at the electrodes and ions moving in the electrolyte.
Supplement: identify the products, and describe the observations, when aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed with inert carbon (graphite) electrodes and with copper electrodes.
Supplement: predict the products at each electrode when dilute or concentrated aqueous solutions of halides are electrolysed.
Supplement: write ionic half-equations for the reactions at the anode (oxidation) and at the cathode (reduction).
State that a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen and that water is its only chemical product.
Supplement: describe the advantages and disadvantages of hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells compared with petrol (gasoline) engines for powering vehicles.
State that an exothermic reaction transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
State that an endothermic reaction takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
Interpret reaction pathway diagrams for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Supplement: state that the thermal energy transferred in a reaction is its enthalpy change, ΔH, which is negative for exothermic reactions and positive for endothermic reactions.
Supplement: define activation energy, Ea, as the minimum energy that colliding particles need in order to react.
Supplement: draw and label reaction pathway diagrams for exothermic and endothermic reactions from given information, showing the reactants, the products, ΔH and Ea.
Supplement: state that breaking bonds is endothermic and making bonds is exothermic, and use this to explain the enthalpy change of a reaction.
Supplement: calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction from bond energies.
Identify physical and chemical changes and describe how they differ.

Describe how the rate of a reaction is affected by changing the concentration of solutions, the pressure of gases, the surface area of solids and the temperature, and by adding or removing a catalyst (including enzymes).
State that a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged at the end of the reaction.
Describe practical methods of investigating the rate of a reaction, including following the change in mass of a reactant or product and the formation of a gas.
Interpret data, including graphs, from rate of reaction experiments.
Supplement: describe collision theory in terms of the number of particles per unit volume, the frequency of collisions, the kinetic energy of the particles and the activation energy, Ea.
Supplement: use collision theory to describe and explain how concentration, gas pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts (including enzymes) affect the rate of a reaction.
Supplement: state that a catalyst lowers the activation energy, Ea, of a reaction.
Supplement: evaluate practical methods of investigating the rate of a reaction, such as measuring a change in mass or the volume of gas formed.
State that some reactions are reversible, shown by the symbol ⇌.

Describe how changing the conditions can change the direction of a reversible reaction, limited to heating hydrated copper(II) sulfate or cobalt(II) chloride and adding water to the anhydrous compounds.

Supplement: state that a reversible reaction in a closed system is at equilibrium when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and the concentrations of reactants and products no longer change.
Supplement: use given information to predict and explain how changing the temperature, pressure or concentration, or using a catalyst, affects the position of equilibrium.
Supplement: state the symbol equation for the production of ammonia in the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
Supplement: state that the hydrogen for the Haber process is obtained from methane and the nitrogen from air.
Supplement: state the typical conditions of the Haber process: 450 °C, 20 000 kPa (200 atm) and an iron catalyst.
Supplement: state the symbol equation for the conversion of sulfur dioxide into sulfur trioxide in the Contact process, 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g).
Supplement: state that the sulfur dioxide is obtained by burning sulfur or roasting sulfide ores and the oxygen from air.
Supplement: state the typical conditions of this conversion: 450 °C, 200 kPa (2 atm) and a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.
Supplement: explain, using ideas about rate and the position of equilibrium together with safety and cost, why the typical conditions are used in the Haber process and the Contact process.
Use a Roman numeral to show the oxidation number of an element in a compound, for example iron(III) chloride.
Define a redox reaction as one in which oxidation and reduction take place at the same time.
Define oxidation as the gain of oxygen and reduction as the loss of oxygen.
Identify redox reactions as reactions in which oxygen is gained by one substance and lost by another.
Identify which substance is oxidised and which is reduced in a redox reaction.
Supplement: define oxidation as the loss of electrons and as an increase in oxidation number.
Supplement: define reduction as the gain of electrons and as a decrease in oxidation number.
Supplement: identify redox reactions as reactions involving the gain and loss of electrons.

Supplement: identify redox reactions from changes in oxidation number, using the rules that an uncombined element has oxidation number zero, a monatomic ion has an oxidation number equal to its charge, the oxidation numbers in a compound add up to zero and those in an ion add up to its charge.
Supplement: identify redox reactions from the colour changes seen with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) or aqueous potassium iodide.
Supplement: define an oxidising agent as a substance that oxidises another substance and is itself reduced.
Supplement: define a reducing agent as a substance that reduces another substance and is itself oxidised.
Supplement: identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in a redox reaction.

children.name: The characteristic properties of acids and bases

objectives.text: Describe the typical reactions of acids with metals, bases and carbonates.
Describe the colours that acids give with litmus, thymolphthalein and methyl orange.
State that bases are oxides or hydroxides of metals and that alkalis are bases that are soluble in water.
Describe the typical reactions of bases with acids and with ammonium salts.
Describe the colours that alkalis give with litmus, thymolphthalein and methyl orange.
State that aqueous solutions of acids contain H⁺ ions and aqueous solutions of alkalis contain OH⁻ ions.
Describe how universal indicator paper colours and pH values are used to compare hydrogen ion concentration, neutrality and how acidic or alkaline solutions are.
Describe the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali as the reaction H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Supplement: define acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors.
Supplement: define a strong acid as one that is completely dissociated in aqueous solution and a weak acid as one that is only partially dissociated.
Supplement: state that hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, shown by HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq).
Supplement: state that ethanoic acid is a weak acid, shown by CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq).
Classify oxides as acidic (including SO₂ and CO₂) or basic (including CuO and CaO), relating this to the metallic or non-metallic character of the element.
Supplement: describe amphoteric oxides as oxides that react with both acids and bases to form a salt and water.
Supplement: classify aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, and zinc oxide, ZnO, as amphoteric.
Describe how to prepare, separate and purify a soluble salt by reacting an acid with an alkali (by titration), or with an excess of a metal, an insoluble base or an insoluble carbonate.

Describe the general solubility rules for salts: sodium, potassium and ammonium salts and all nitrates are soluble; chlorides are soluble except those of lead and silver; sulfates are soluble except those of barium, calcium and lead; carbonates are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium; hydroxides are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium, with calcium hydroxide partially soluble.
Define a hydrated substance as one that is chemically combined with water and an anhydrous substance as one that contains no water.
Supplement: describe how an insoluble salt is prepared by precipitation.
Supplement: define water of crystallisation as the water molecules present in hydrated crystals, such as CuSO₄·5H₂O and CoCl₂·6H₂O.
Describe the Periodic Table as an arrangement of the elements in periods and groups in order of increasing proton (atomic) number.
Describe how the elements change from metallic to non-metallic character across a period.
Describe how the group number is related to the charge on the ions formed by elements in that group.
Explain, in terms of electronic configuration, why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
Explain how the position of an element in the Periodic Table can be used to predict its properties.
Supplement: identify trends in a group from information given about its elements.
Describe lithium, sodium and potassium as relatively soft metals whose general trends down the group are decreasing melting point, increasing density and increasing reactivity.
Predict the properties of other Group I elements from information given about them.
Describe chlorine, bromine and iodine as diatomic non-metals whose general trends down the group are increasing density and decreasing reactivity.
State the appearance of the halogens at room temperature and pressure: chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid and iodine a grey-black solid.
Describe and explain the displacement reactions of halogens with solutions of other halide ions.
Predict the properties of other Group VII elements from information given about them.
Describe the transition elements as metals that have high densities and high melting points, form coloured compounds and often act as catalysts, both as elements and in their compounds.
Supplement: describe transition elements as forming ions with variable oxidation numbers, including iron(II) and iron(III).
Describe the Group VIII noble gases as unreactive, monatomic gases and explain this in terms of their electronic configuration.
Compare the general physical properties of metals and non-metals, including thermal and electrical conductivity, malleability and ductility, and melting and boiling points.
Describe the general chemical properties of metals, limited to their reactions with dilute acids, with cold water and steam, and with oxygen.

Describe uses of metals linked to their physical properties: aluminium for aircraft (low density), for overhead power cables (low density and good electrical conductivity) and for food containers (resistance to corrosion), and copper for electrical wiring (good electrical conductivity and ductility).
Describe an alloy as a mixture of a metal with other elements, including brass (copper and zinc) and stainless steel (iron with elements such as chromium, nickel and carbon).
State that alloys can be harder and stronger than the pure metals and are therefore more useful.
Describe uses of alloys linked to their physical properties, including stainless steel for cutlery because it is hard and resists rusting.
Identify diagrams that represent the structure of an alloy.
Supplement: explain, in terms of structure, that alloys can be harder and stronger than pure metals because atoms of different sizes stop the layers sliding over each other.
State the order of the reactivity series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold.

Describe the reactions, if any, of potassium, sodium and calcium with cold water, of magnesium with steam, and of magnesium, zinc, iron, copper, silver and gold with dilute hydrochloric acid, and explain them by the positions of the metals in the reactivity series.
Deduce an order of reactivity from a set of experimental results.

Supplement: describe the relative reactivity of metals as their tendency to form positive ions, shown by their displacement reactions, if any, with aqueous ions of magnesium, zinc, iron, copper and silver.
Supplement: explain why aluminium appears unreactive in terms of its oxide layer.
State the conditions needed for iron and steel to rust, forming hydrated iron(III) oxide.
State common barrier methods of preventing rusting, including painting, greasing and coating with plastic.
Describe how barrier methods prevent rusting by keeping out oxygen or water.
Supplement: describe galvanising with zinc as an example of both a barrier method and sacrificial protection.
Supplement: explain sacrificial protection in terms of the reactivity series and of electron loss.
Describe how the ease of obtaining a metal from its ore is related to the metal's position in the reactivity series.

Describe the extraction of iron from haematite (hematite) in the blast furnace: burning coke to provide heat and carbon dioxide, reducing carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide, reducing iron(III) oxide with carbon monoxide, thermally decomposing limestone to calcium oxide and forming slag (symbol equations are not required).
State that bauxite is the main ore of aluminium and that aluminium is extracted by electrolysis.
Supplement: state the symbol equations for the reactions in the blast furnace: C + O₂ → CO₂, C + CO₂ → 2CO, Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ and CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃.

Supplement: describe the extraction of aluminium from purified bauxite (aluminium oxide), including the role of cryolite, why the carbon anodes must be replaced regularly and the electrode reactions with ionic half-equations (details of purifying bauxite are not required).
Describe chemical tests for the presence of water using anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride and anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
Describe how melting point and boiling point are used to test whether water is pure.
Explain why distilled water rather than tap water is used in practical chemistry: it contains fewer chemical impurities.
State that water from natural sources may contain dissolved oxygen, metal compounds, plastics, sewage, harmful microbes, nitrates from fertilisers and phosphates from fertilisers and detergents.
State that some of these substances are beneficial, such as dissolved oxygen for aquatic life and metal compounds that provide essential minerals for life.

State that some of these substances are potentially harmful: some metal compounds are toxic, some plastics harm aquatic life, sewage contains microbes that cause disease, and nitrates and phosphates lead to deoxygenation of water and damage to aquatic life (details of eutrophication are not required).
Describe how the domestic water supply is treated: sedimentation and filtration to remove solids, carbon to remove tastes and odours, and chlorination to kill microbes.
State that ammonium salts and nitrates are used as fertilisers.
Describe how NPK fertilisers supply the elements nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium for better plant growth.
State that clean, dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with the remainder a mixture of noble gases and carbon dioxide.

State the sources of the air pollutants carbon dioxide (complete combustion of carbon-containing fuels), carbon monoxide and particulates (incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels), methane (decomposition of vegetation and waste gases from digestion in animals), oxides of nitrogen (car engines) and sulfur dioxide (burning fossil fuels that contain sulfur compounds).

State the harmful effects of these pollutants: more carbon dioxide and methane increase global warming, leading to climate change; carbon monoxide is toxic; particulates increase the risk of respiratory problems and cancer; oxides of nitrogen cause acid rain, photochemical smog and respiratory problems; sulfur dioxide causes acid rain.

State and explain ways of reducing climate change (planting trees, less livestock farming, less use of fossil fuels, more use of hydrogen and renewable energy such as wind and solar) and acid rain (catalytic converters in vehicles, low-sulfur fuels and flue-gas desulfurisation with calcium oxide).
Describe photosynthesis as the reaction between carbon dioxide and water, using energy from light in the presence of chlorophyll, to produce glucose and oxygen.
State the word equation for photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.
Supplement: describe how carbon dioxide and methane cause global warming through the absorption, reflection and emission of thermal energy, which reduces the loss of thermal energy to space.
Supplement: explain how oxides of nitrogen form in car engines and describe their removal by catalytic converters, for example 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂.
Supplement: state the symbol equation for photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
Draw and interpret displayed formulae, showing every atom and every bond in a molecule.
Write and interpret the general formulae of the homologous series of alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂), alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ), alcohols (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH) and carboxylic acids (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH).
Identify a functional group as the atom or group of atoms that determines the chemical properties of a homologous series.
State that a homologous series is a family of similar compounds with similar chemical properties because they have the same functional group.
State that a saturated compound has molecules in which all the carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds.
State that an unsaturated compound has molecules in which one or more carbon–carbon bonds are not single bonds.
Supplement: state that a structural formula shows unambiguously how the atoms in a molecule are arranged, for example CH₂=CH₂, CH₃CH₂OH and CH₃COOCH₃.

Supplement: define structural isomers as compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₃ for C₄H₁₀, and CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂ and CH₃CH=CHCH₃ for C₄H₈.

Supplement: describe the general characteristics of a homologous series: the same functional group and general formula, successive members differing by a –CH₂– unit, a trend in physical properties and similar chemical properties.
Name and draw the displayed formulae of methane, ethane, ethene, ethanol, ethanoic acid and the products of the reactions in sections 11.4 to 11.7.
State the type of compound present from a name ending in -ane, -ene, -ol or -oic acid, or from a molecular or displayed formula.

Supplement: name and draw the structural and displayed formulae of unbranched alkanes, alkenes (including but-1-ene and but-2-ene), alcohols (including propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol, butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol) and carboxylic acids with up to four carbon atoms per molecule.
Supplement: name and draw the displayed formulae of the unbranched esters made from unbranched alcohols and carboxylic acids that each have up to four carbon atoms.
Name coal, natural gas and petroleum as fossil fuels.
Name methane as the main constituent of natural gas.
State that hydrocarbons are compounds that contain hydrogen and carbon only.
State that petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons.
Describe how petroleum is separated into useful fractions by fractional distillation.
Describe how the fractions change from the bottom to the top of the fractionating column: shorter chains, higher volatility, lower boiling points and lower viscosity.

Name the uses of the fractions: refinery gas for heating and cooking; gasoline (petrol) for cars; naphtha as a chemical feedstock; kerosene (paraffin) for jet fuel; diesel oil (gas oil) for diesel engines; fuel oil for ships and home heating; lubricating oil for lubricants, waxes and polishes; bitumen for making roads.
State that the bonding in alkanes is single covalent bonds and that alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons.
Describe alkanes as generally unreactive, apart from combustion and substitution by chlorine.
Supplement: state that in a substitution reaction one atom or group of atoms is replaced by another atom or group of atoms.

Supplement: describe the substitution reaction of alkanes with chlorine as a photochemical reaction in which ultraviolet light provides the activation energy, and draw the structural or displayed formulae of the products (monosubstitution only).
State that the bonding in alkenes includes a carbon–carbon double covalent bond and that alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Describe how alkenes and hydrogen are manufactured by cracking larger alkane molecules at a high temperature with a catalyst.
Describe the reasons for cracking larger alkane molecules.
Describe how reaction with aqueous bromine distinguishes saturated from unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Supplement: state that an addition reaction forms only one product.

Supplement: describe the addition reactions of alkenes with bromine or aqueous bromine, with hydrogen (nickel catalyst) and with steam (acid catalyst), and draw the structural or displayed formulae of the products.

Describe the manufacture of ethanol by fermentation of aqueous glucose with yeast at 25–35 °C in the absence of oxygen, and by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene at 300 °C and 6000 kPa (60 atm) with an acid catalyst.
Describe the combustion of ethanol.
State that ethanol is used as a solvent and as a fuel.
Supplement: describe the advantages and disadvantages of manufacturing ethanol by fermentation and by the catalytic addition of steam to ethene.
Describe the reactions of ethanoic acid with metals, bases and carbonates, including the names and formulae of the salts formed.
Supplement: describe the formation of ethanoic acid by oxidising ethanol with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) and by bacterial oxidation during vinegar production.
Supplement: describe the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, using an acid catalyst, to form an ester.
Define polymers as large molecules built up from many smaller molecules called monomers.
Describe the formation of poly(ethene) from ethene monomers as an example of addition polymerisation.
State that plastics are made from polymers.
Describe how the properties of plastics affect how they can be disposed of.
Describe the environmental problems caused by plastics: disposal in landfill sites, build-up in the oceans and toxic gases formed when they are burned.
Supplement: identify the repeat units and linkages in addition polymers and in condensation polymers.
Supplement: deduce the structure or repeat unit of an addition polymer from a given alkene, and the alkene from a given polymer.

Supplement: deduce the structure or repeat unit of a condensation polymer from given monomers, and the monomers from a given polymer, limited to polyamides (from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine) and polyesters (from a dicarboxylic acid and a diol).
Supplement: describe the differences between addition and condensation polymerisation.
Supplement: describe and draw the structures of nylon (a polyamide) and PET (a polyester); the full chemical name of PET is not required.
Supplement: state that PET can be converted back into its monomers and polymerised again.
Supplement: describe proteins as natural polyamides formed from amino acid monomers with the general structure H₂N–CHR–COOH, where R is a side chain that differs between amino acids.
Supplement: describe and draw the structure of a protein as amino acid units joined by amide linkages.

children.name: Experimental design
children.description: Also the home of the practical skills assessed in Papers 5 and 6 (section 4 of the syllabus: planning, measuring, recording, interpreting and evaluating).

objectives.text: Name suitable apparatus for measuring time, temperature, mass and volume, including stop-watches, thermometers, balances, burettes, volumetric pipettes, measuring cylinders and gas syringes.
Suggest advantages and disadvantages of experimental methods and apparatus.
Describe the meaning of solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution (the maximum concentration of solute at a stated temperature), residue and filtrate.
Describe an acid–base titration using a burette, a volumetric pipette and a suitable indicator.
Describe how an indicator is used to identify the end-point of a titration.
Describe how paper chromatography with a suitable solvent separates mixtures of soluble coloured substances.
Interpret simple chromatograms to identify unknown substances by comparison with known substances and to tell pure from impure substances.

Supplement: describe how paper chromatography separates mixtures of soluble colourless substances using a suitable solvent and a locating agent (knowledge of specific locating agents is not required).
Supplement: state and use Rf = distance travelled by the substance ÷ distance travelled by the solvent.
Describe and explain separation and purification using a suitable solvent, filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation and fractional distillation.
Suggest suitable techniques to separate and purify substances, given information about them.
Identify substances and judge their purity using melting point and boiling point information.

Describe tests for the anions carbonate (react with dilute acid, then test for carbon dioxide), chloride, bromide and iodide (acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate), nitrate (reduce with aluminium foil and aqueous sodium hydroxide, then test for ammonia), sulfate (acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate) and sulfite (react with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII)).
Describe tests with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to identify the aqueous cations aluminium, ammonium, calcium, chromium(III), copper(II), iron(II), iron(III) and zinc.

Describe tests for the gases ammonia (damp red litmus paper), carbon dioxide (limewater), chlorine (damp litmus paper), hydrogen (lighted splint), oxygen (glowing splint) and sulfur dioxide (acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII)).
Describe how a flame test identifies the cations lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, barium and copper(II).
